lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Dejair Caitano do Nascimento | Lesson 20 -- Bangkok Ready

listenings.text: Hi! Are you here for the pain congress too? I saw your name badge in the elevator. I'm Arjun, I work in Chennai, in a neurology department. I arrived at six this morning, so my jet lag is terrible. Honestly, I'm running on empty. Have you been to the plenary yet? People say it's going to be packed, so we should get there early. Where are you based, by the way?

Thank you for your presentation. I have to be honest, I am not completely convinced. You have sixty patients, and only one center. That is a very small sample. In my experience, with a sample like this, the effect you found could simply be chance. Also, all your patients come from one region of Brazil, so how can you say this is true for patients in Asia or in Europe? I am not saying your finding is wrong. I am saying it is preliminary. So my question is simple: what do you plan to do next to show that the result is real?

It was really nice to talk to you at lunch. I think our projects are quite similar. We are also looking at nerve damage, but in patients with diabetes. I would love to read your paper when it comes out. Here is my business card, my email is on the back. If you send me your protocol, I will share our data with you. And if you come to Istanbul next year, let me know, and we can meet. Have a good flight home!

reading.rtitle: Five Scenes of a Congress Day
paras: A congress day is not one long talk. It is a series of short scenes, and each scene needs different English. The day usually starts before the first session: in the hotel elevator, at the registration desk, in the line for coffee. Here people make small talk. It is short and friendly, and nobody expects perfect grammar. A simple question is enough: Where are you based? Is this your first time in Bangkok?

Then comes the plenary, with the whole congress in one big room, and after it the breakout sessions, in smaller rooms. This is where the hard questions come. Somebody may challenge your data or ask two questions at once. The best answer is calm: repair if you need to, agree with what is true, and explain your next step. Sessions often run late, so keep your answer short.

The most important scene is often the last one: lunch, the coffee break or the poster area at the end of the day. Here people exchange business cards and decide who they want to work with. A good follow-up sentence turns a conversation into a collaboration: If you send me your protocol, I'll share our data. Before you wrap up, ask for a contact. A congress is three days long, but a good contact can last for years.
reading.source: Written for this class from common advice for researchers at international congresses.
